lessons.title: Printing in Java
objectives: print a line of text with System.out.println
stack several printed lines to build a screen
keep the cursor on the same line with System.out.print

steps.instruction: We're building a game's title screen.

points.label: the screen
points.text: A title, a menu of choices, and a prompt asking the player to pick one.

points.label: all of it is text
points.text: Every line you have ever seen a program print is just text it was told to print.

points.label: one command
points.text: You need exactly one new thing to build the whole screen. We start with it now.

steps.instruction: This is the command that puts text on the screen.
steps.code: System.out.println("*** DUNGEON QUEST ***");

points.label: System.out.println
points.text: Spelled exactly like that. Capital S, everything else lowercase, no spaces.

points.label: the quotes
points.text: Whatever sits between the double quotes is what appears. Java does not read it — it just prints it.

points.label: the quotes vanish
points.text: They mark where the text starts and stops. They never show up in the output.

points.label: the semicolon
points.text: Ends the instruction. Every line like this needs one.

steps.instruction: Run it. There is your title.
steps.code: System.out.println("*** DUNGEON QUEST ***");
steps.after: One command, one line on screen.

steps.instruction: Rename the game to SPACE RAIDER.
steps.code: System.out.println("*** DUNGEON QUEST ***");
steps.hint: Only the text between the quotes changes.
steps.after: Your game, your title.
skills: print a line of text with System.out.println

steps.instruction: Add the menu. Each println starts a new line.

points.label: three commands
points.text: Three printlns, three lines. They run top to bottom, in order.

points.label: ln
points.text: The ln on the end means "then move to the next line". That is why they stack instead of running together.

points.label: the spaces count
points.text: The two spaces before 1. are inside the quotes, so they get printed too. That is how the menu is indented.

steps.instruction: Run it. The screen is taking shape.
steps.after: Order matters — they print in the order you wrote them.
skills: stack several printed lines to build a screen

steps.instruction: A gap under the title makes it readable.

points.label: println("")
points.text: Nothing between the quotes, so it prints nothing — then moves to the next line anyway.

points.label: the result
points.text: An empty line. That is all a blank line is: a line with nothing on it.

points.label: spacing is design
points.text: Same words, easier to read. Where you put gaps is a real decision.

steps.instruction: The last line is different — the player types right after it.
steps.output:
*** DUNGEON QUEST ***

  1. New game
  2. Quit

Choose 1-2:

points.label: print, no ln
points.text: Prints and STAYS on the line. The cursor waits right after the text.

points.label: why here
points.text: A prompt should have the answer next to it, not on the line below. Choose 1-2: 2 reads properly.

points.label: the space
points.text: The space after the colon is inside the quotes, so the answer will not touch the question mark.

points.label: the difference
points.text: print and println are the same command. The only difference is whether the line ends.

steps.instruction: Two prints in a row this time. What comes out?
steps.why: Neither print ends its line, so all three land on one line. Only the final println ends it.
skills: keep the cursor on the same line with System.out.print

steps.instruction: Run the finished title screen.
steps.after: You built a whole screen out of one command and its no-newline twin.
skills: stack several printed lines to build a screen

steps.instruction: The exact rules, so they hold up in a test.

points.label: the spelling
points.text: System.out.println. Not printLine, not System.println, not print alone. Java accepts nothing else.

points.label: println
points.text: Prints, then ENDS the line.

points.label: print
points.text: Prints, and LEAVES the line open. The next thing continues right after it.

points.label: so
points.text: Line 1 ended. Lines 2 and 3 share a line, because line 2 never ended.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code: System.out.println("Hello Karel");

questions.prompt: Which one actually prints in Java?
questions.why: println is all lowercase, and it has to be System.out in front. The other three do not exist.

questions.prompt: System.out.println("Hello"); then System.out.println("World"); prints how many lines?
questions.why: Each println ends its own line, so the two words land on separate lines.

skills: print a line of text with System.out.println

steps.instruction: This one will not run. Something is missing.
steps.code: System.out.println(Game over);
steps.solution: System.out.println("Game over");
steps.hint: Text has to be wrapped in double quotes, or Java tries to read it as code.
steps.after: Without quotes Java thinks Game and over are things you defined. They are not.
skills: print a line of text with System.out.println

steps.instruction: Tap the lines in order to make the output below.
steps.hint: print keeps the line open. println closes it.
steps.after: You now control exactly where each line breaks.
skills: keep the cursor on the same line with System.out.print

steps.instruction: Introduce yourself in two lines.
steps.code: // line 1 says your name, line 2 says what you like
steps.target:
My name is Ada.
I like comedy.
steps.solution:
System.out.println("My name is Ada.");
System.out.println("I like comedy.");
steps.hint: Two printlns. Line 1 must contain the word name, line 2 the word like.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.1.5, Welcome Program.
skills: stack several printed lines to build a screen

steps.instruction: Last one: draw this exactly.
steps.code: // four printlns, one per line of the drawing
steps.hint: One println per line. The spaces at the start of each line go inside the quotes.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.1.6, ASCII Art. Lesson done.
skills: stack several printed lines to build a screen

lessons.title: Variables and Types
objectives: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name
use = to put a value in, and change it later
choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: We're building a player card.

points.label: the card
points.text: Five facts about one player: their name, their level, their health, their rank, and whether they are online.

points.label: the problem
points.text: Each fact is a different KIND of thing. A name is text. A level is a whole number. Health can be half a heart.

points.label: a variable
points.text: A labelled box that holds one fact. You put a value in once, then use the label wherever you need it.

points.label: how we go
points.text: One box at a time. The card grows on screen, and by the end you have built the whole thing.

steps.instruction: First fact: the name. Text goes in a String.

points.label: String name
points.text: The type goes in FRONT of the name you choose. That is what creates the box.

points.label: = "Ada"
points.text: The = does not mean "equals". It means "put this in". The text goes into the box.

points.label: String
points.text: Capital S. Holds text of any length, in double quotes.

points.label: the + sign
points.text: Joins text together. "Name:   " is spelled out by you; name is fetched from the box. The + glues them into one line.

points.label: no quotes on name
points.text: With quotes, "name" would print the word. Without them, Java goes and gets what is inside the box.

steps.instruction: Run it. That is the first line of the card.
steps.after: One box made, one line printed.

steps.instruction: Make the player Grace instead.
steps.hint: Only the text inside the quotes changes.
steps.after: One edit changed the card. The label stayed the same.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: Next fact: the level. Whole numbers go in an int.

points.label: int level
points.text: Same shape as before: type, name, =, value.

points.label: int
points.text: Whole numbers only. 7, 0, -3. No decimal point.

points.label: no quotes
points.text: 7 is a number, so it needs no quotes. "7" with quotes would be text.

points.label: the card grows
points.text: Two boxes now, two lines of card.

steps.instruction: The player levels up. Changing a box is not the same as making one.

points.label: int level = 7;
points.text: Type in FRONT, so this MAKES the box. This is called declaring, and you do it once.

points.label: level = 8;
points.text: No type. The box already exists, so this only puts a new value in.

points.label: the 7 is gone
points.text: A box holds one value. Putting 8 in throws the 7 away — it does not add up.

points.label: int level = 8;
points.text: Writing that second line WITH the type would be an error: you cannot make the same box twice.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: The second line replaces what is in the box. It does not add — 7 and 8 never meet.
skills: use = to put a value in, and change it later

steps.instruction: Next fact: health. Half a heart will not fit in an int.
steps.output:
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5

points.label: the problem
points.text: Health is 2.5 hearts. An int has nowhere to keep the .5, so it cannot hold it.

points.label: double
points.text: Works exactly like int, but it keeps the decimal part.

points.label: which to pick
points.text: int for what you COUNT: levels, lives, coins. double for what you MEASURE: health, height, money.

points.label: still fine
points.text: A double can hold a whole number too. It just shows it as 3.0 instead of 3.

steps.instruction: This one refuses to run. Fix the type.
steps.code:
int health = 2.5;
System.out.println("Health: " + health);
steps.solution:
double health = 2.5;
System.out.println("Health: " + health);
steps.hint: 2.5 has a decimal point. Which type keeps that?
steps.after: Java refused rather than quietly losing your .5. That refusal is it protecting you.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Next fact: the rank, a single letter.
steps.output:
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5
Rank:   A

points.label: char
points.text: Exactly ONE character. A letter, a digit, a symbol — one.

points.label: 'A'
points.text: SINGLE quotes. 'A' is a char. "A" with double quotes would be a String.

points.label: why bother
points.text: A rank is always one letter, so char says so exactly. A name could be any length, so it stays a String.

steps.instruction: Last fact: are they online? That is a yes or a no.
steps.output:
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5
Rank:   A
Online: true

points.label: boolean
points.text: Holds only true or false. Nothing else is allowed in the box.

points.label: lowercase, no quotes
points.text: true, not True, and not "true" — quotes would make it text.

points.label: card complete
points.text: Five facts, five types. Every one chosen because of what it had to hold.

steps.instruction: Run the finished card.
steps.after: You built that from one line. Five boxes, five kinds of value.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Now the exact rules, so they hold up in a test.

points.label: four parts
points.text: Every declaration is: TYPE, NAME, =, VALUE. In that order, ending in a semicolon.

points.label: declare once
points.text: The type appears only the first time. After that, just name = value.

points.label: capitals matter
points.text: level and Level are two different boxes. Java will not guess what you meant.

points.label: quotes decide the type
points.text: "A" is a String. 'A' is a char. A is a variable name. Same letter, three meanings.

steps.instruction: Which type holds each value?
steps.why: Whole number → int. Decimal → double. One character in single quotes → char. Text in double quotes → String. true/false → boolean.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a type Java has?
questions.why: int, double, char and boolean are all built into Java. apple is just a word — Java has never heard of it.

questions.prompt: Which line both MAKES a box and puts a value in?
questions.why: It has all four parts: type, name, =, value. The second only changes an existing box; the third has no name; the fourth is just text.

skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: Put the right type in front of each name.
steps.hint: Text in double quotes, then a whole number.
steps.after: Type in front, every time.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: This will not run. Look carefully at the capitals.
steps.code:
int Level = 7;
System.out.println("Level:  " + level);
steps.solution:
int level = 7;
System.out.println("Level:  " + level);
steps.hint: Level and level are two different names as far as Java is concerned.
steps.after: One capital letter is enough to break it. Java never guesses.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: a = b copies the value. Follow it.

questions.why: a = b copies what is currently in b, which is 2.
Still 2. Copying took the value, not the box — changing b later does nothing to a.

skills: use = to put a value in, and change it later

steps.instruction: Fill in the two missing values so it prints the card below.
steps.hint: Text needs double quotes. A whole number needs none.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.2.5, Answering Questions.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Last one: store the year in an int, then print the sentence.
steps.code: // declare an int called year, then print it
steps.solution:
int year = 2026;
System.out.println("The current year is " + year);
steps.hint: Type, name, =, value. Then join text and the box with a +.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.2.4, Our First Integer. Lesson done.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

lessons.title: User Input
objectives: read what the user types with readLine
choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean
use a value the user typed in the rest of the program

steps.instruction: Last lesson you built a player card. It always says Ada.

points.label: the problem
points.text: Every value is typed into the code. To play as someone else you have to edit the program.

points.label: real games
points.text: A real game asks YOU. You type your name, it puts it on the card.

points.label: what we need
points.text: A way to stop, wait for the player to type something, and keep what they typed.

points.label: today
points.text: We turn the card into a character creator. Same card, filled in by whoever is playing.

steps.instruction: readLine asks a question and hands back the answer.
steps.output:
Your name? Ada
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada

points.label: readLine
points.text: Stops the program, waits for the player to type, and gives back whatever they typed.

points.label: the question goes inside
points.text: "Your name? " sits in the brackets. You do NOT print it separately — readLine prints it for you.

points.label: String name =
points.text: The answer is text, so it goes into a String box. Same four parts as always: type, name, =, value.

points.label: read the output
points.text: Line 1 is the question with Ada typed after it. The card below uses that same Ada.

steps.instruction: Run it. We'll type Ada for you.
steps.after: The program waited, took the answer, and used it.
skills: read what the user types with readLine

steps.instruction: Change the question to "Who are you? "
steps.target:
Who are you? Ada
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
steps.hint: The question is the text inside readLine's brackets. Keep the space before the closing quote.
steps.after: You decide exactly what the player is asked.
skills: read what the user types with readLine

steps.instruction: The level has to be a number, so it needs a different reader.
steps.output:
Your name? Ada
Starting level? 7
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7

points.label: readInt
points.text: Same idea as readLine, but it hands back a whole number instead of text.

points.label: why it matters
points.text: A level gets added to later. readLine would give you the TEXT "7", and text cannot do maths.

points.label: the box matches
points.text: readInt gives an int, so it goes in an int. The reader and the box always agree.

points.label: same shape
points.text: Question in the brackets, answer comes back. All four readers work this way.

steps.instruction: The player types 10. What appears?
steps.code:
int level = readInt("Level? ");
System.out.println(level);
steps.why: Line 1 is the question with 10 typed straight after it, because the question does not end its line. Line 2 is the println.
skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean

steps.instruction: Health can be half a heart, so it needs the decimal reader.
steps.output:
Your name? Ada
Starting level? 7
Starting health? 2.5
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5

points.label: readDouble
points.text: Hands back a number that can have a decimal point.

points.label: match the type
points.text: readDouble → double, exactly like readInt → int. Pick the reader that matches the box you want.

points.label: three so far
points.text: Text, whole number, decimal. One left.

steps.instruction: Last one: a yes or no answer.
steps.output:
Your name? Ada
Starting level? 7
Starting health? 2.5
Online now? true
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5
Online: true

points.label: readBoolean
points.text: Hands back true or false. The player types the word true or the word false.

points.label: the set is complete
points.text: readLine, readInt, readDouble, readBoolean. There are four, and that is all of them.

points.label: creator done
points.text: Every value on the card now comes from whoever is playing.

steps.instruction: Run the finished character creator.
steps.after: Four questions, four types, one card. That is a real program.
skills: use a value the user typed in the rest of the program

steps.instruction: The exact rules, so they hold up in a test.

points.label: four readers, no more
points.text: readLine → String. readInt → int. readDouble → double. readBoolean → boolean. There is no readChar.

points.label: the prompt is an argument
points.text: It goes inside the brackets. Printing it on a separate line first is a different, worse program.

points.label: no line break
points.text: The question does not end its line, so what the player types appears right after it. That is deliberate.

points.label: box must match
points.text: The reader decides the type. Put readInt in a String and Java refuses.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a real input method?
questions.why: There are exactly four, and readChar is not one of them. A single character comes back as a String.

questions.prompt: int n = readInt("Number "); then println(n). The user types 10. What prints after the question?
questions.why: readInt hands back the number itself. Printing it shows 10 — not the variable name, and not with quotes.

skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean

steps.instruction: Match each reader to what it hands back.
steps.why: The name tells you the type it returns, and that decides the box you need.
skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean

steps.instruction: A name is not a number. Fix the reader.
steps.code:
String name = readInt("Your name? ");
System.out.println("Hi, " + name + "!");
steps.solution:
String name = readLine("Your name? ");
System.out.println("Hi, " + name + "!");
steps.hint: Which of the four hands back text?
steps.after: The reader has to match the kind of answer, and the box has to match the reader.
skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean

steps.instruction: Pick the reader for each question.
steps.hint: An age is whole. A price is not.
steps.after: Reader, box, and the kind of answer all have to agree.
skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean

steps.instruction: Last one: ask three questions, then print the three answers.
steps.code: // ask about food, colour and movie, then print all three
steps.target:
What is your favorite food? pasta
What is your favorite color? green
What is your favorite movie? Moana
pasta
green
Moana
steps.hint: Three readLine calls first, storing each answer, then three printlns. Questions are "What is your favorite food? " and so on.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.3.4, About You. Lesson done.
skills: use a value the user typed in the rest of the program

lessons.title: Arithmetic Expressions
objectives: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
predict the result of whole-number division
use the remainder operator to find what is left over

steps.instruction: Your party just found a pile of loot. Time to split it.

points.label: the job
points.text: 17 coins, 5 players. How many does each one get, and what is left in the pot?

points.label: why it is not obvious
points.text: You cannot hand out a third of a coin. Java has a particular idea about this, and it surprises people.

points.label: on the way
points.text: We do the ordinary maths first — buying, totals — then get to the splitting.

steps.instruction: Java does maths with the symbols you already know.

points.label: + and -
points.text: Add and subtract, exactly as you would expect.
Multiply. A star, not an × — there is no × key on a keyboard.

points.label: boxes work too
points.text: gold + found uses what is inside each box. The maths happens on the values.

points.label: nothing changed
points.text: Printing gold + found does not alter gold. It works out an answer and prints it.

steps.instruction: Run it.
steps.after: Three sums, three answers.

steps.instruction: Buying two potions and a sword — order matters.

points.label: 2 * potion + sword
points.text: Two potions at 3 gold, plus one sword at 10.

points.label: * goes first
points.text: Multiply and divide happen before add and subtract — the same rule as maths class.

points.label: so
points.text: 2 * 3 is 6, then 6 + 10 is 16. It is NOT 2 * 13.

points.label: brackets win
points.text: Anything in brackets is worked out first, before everything else.

steps.instruction: Brackets added. Now what?
steps.why: The brackets force potion + sword first: 3 + 10 is 13, then 2 * 13 is 26. Same numbers, different answer.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations

steps.instruction: Now the split. This is the one that catches everybody.

points.text: In maths that is 3.4. Java says 3.

points.label: why
points.text: Both numbers are whole numbers, so Java keeps the answer whole. It does not round — it throws the rest away.

points.label: it fits the job
points.text: You cannot hand out 0.4 of a coin, so 3 each is actually the right answer here.

points.label: but
points.text: Something IS left over, and Java just dropped it. Getting it back is the next step.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.code: System.out.println(9 / 2);
steps.why: Two whole numbers, so the answer stays whole. 4.5 chops down to 4 — it never rounds up.
skills: predict the result of whole-number division

steps.instruction: % gives you exactly what was left over.

points.text: The remainder. Read it as "what is left after dividing".
5 goes into 17 three times, using 15 coins. 2 are left. So 2.

points.label: the pair
points.text: / tells you how many each. % tells you what stays in the pot. Together they split anything.
A remainder of 0 means it divided evenly. That is how you will test for even numbers later.

steps.instruction: One more thing: changing a number you already have.

points.label: gold += 12
points.text: Short for gold = gold + 12. Take what is in the box, add 12, put it back.

points.label: gold++
points.text: Short for gold = gold + 1. Adds exactly one.

points.label: the others
points.text: -= takes away, *= multiplies, /= divides. Same pattern every time.

points.label: why you care
points.text: You will see ++ constantly once loops start. This is where it comes from.

steps.instruction: Run the finished loot split.
steps.after: Three each, two in the pot. That is the whole job done with / and %.
skills: use the remainder operator to find what is left over

steps.instruction: The exact rules, so they hold up in a test.

points.text: Two whole numbers, whole answer: 3. The .5 is gone, not rounded.
One decimal is enough to make the whole thing decimal: 3.5.
The remainder: 1. That is the .5 you lost, expressed as what was left.

points.label: precedence
points.text: Brackets, then * / %, then + -. Same-level operations run left to right.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code:
int a = 150;
int b = 100;

questions.why: 100 goes into 150 once, using 100. 50 is left over.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a Java arithmetic operator?
questions.why: Java uses + - * / and %. The # symbol means nothing to it.

skills: use the remainder operator to find what is left over

steps.instruction: Fill it in so it splits 17 into boxes of 5.
steps.hint: First how many fit, then what refuses to fit.
steps.after: / and % are a pair. You will almost always want both.
skills: predict the result of whole-number division

steps.instruction: One decimal in the sum. What now?
steps.code: System.out.println(9 / 2.0);
steps.why: 2.0 is a decimal, so Java keeps the decimal answer. Compare with 9 / 2, which gave 4.
skills: predict the result of whole-number division

steps.instruction: Last one: work out what a pyramid weighs. Each block is 2.5 tons.
steps.code: // ask how many blocks, then print the weight
steps.target:
Enter the number of blocks used to build the pyramid: 3
The pyramid weighs 7.5 tons
steps.solution:
int blocks = readInt("Enter the number of blocks used to build the pyramid: ");
System.out.println("The pyramid weighs " + (blocks * 2.5) + " tons");
steps.hint: Read the count with readInt, multiply by 2.5, and join it into the sentence. Keep the brackets around the sum.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.4.5, Weight of a Pyramid. Lesson done.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations

lessons.title: Casting
objectives: use (double) so whole-number division keeps its decimal
use (int) to turn a decimal into a whole number
round to the nearest whole number using casting

steps.instruction: Your character has 7 XP. The next level needs 20.

points.label: the readout
points.text: We want the bar to say Progress: 35% — the share of the way there, as a whole number.

points.label: the sum
points.text: 7 out of 20 is 7 / 20, times 100. Straightforward maths.

points.label: the catch
points.text: Written the obvious way in Java, that prints 0. Not 35, not 0.35 — zero.

points.label: this lesson
points.text: Why it does that, and the one tool that fixes it.

steps.instruction: Here it is going wrong. Watch closely.

points.label: 7 / 20 first
points.text: Division happens before multiplication? No — they are equal, so it runs left to right. 7 / 20 goes first.

points.label: both are ints
points.text: From last lesson: two whole numbers give a whole answer. 7 / 20 is 0.35, so Java gives 0.

points.label: then 0 * 100
points.text: Zero times anything is zero. The answer was already destroyed before the 100 arrived.

points.label: the real problem
points.text: Nothing is broken. Java did exactly what int division always does — it just was not what we wanted.

steps.instruction: Run it and see the 0 for yourself.
steps.after: A correct program giving a useless answer. Now we fix it.

steps.instruction: Casting tells Java to treat a value as a different type.

points.label: (double)
points.text: The type you want, in brackets, in front of the value. Here it turns 7 into 7.0.

steps.instruction: That is the rule worth remembering.

points.label: cast before, not after
points.text: (double) x / y works. (double) (x / y) does not. The cast has to reach the division before it happens.

points.label: why
points.text: Once two ints divide, the fraction is gone. Casting afterwards converts a number that is already wrong.

points.label: how to read it
points.text: A cast only applies to the thing immediately after it. Brackets change what that thing is.

points.label: it chops
points.text: 35.9 becomes 35. Everything after the point is thrown away — it does NOT round.

points.label: even 35.999

points.label: rounding down still works
points.text: 37.4 + 0.5 is 37.9, which chops to 37. Correct.

points.label: exactly .5 goes up
points.text: That is the rule you were taught in maths, and this reproduces it.

points.label: the brackets matter
points.text: The + 0.5 must happen before the chop, so it needs its own brackets inside the cast.

lessons.title: Booleans
objectives: create boolean variables that hold true or false
tell a boolean apart from text, a character and a number
read a true/false answer from the user

steps.instruction: A game is full of facts that are simply yes or no.

points.label: the panel
points.text: Is the player alive? Do they have the key? Is the quest finished? We are building that status screen.

points.label: not a number
points.text: None of these is a count or a measurement. There is no "3 alive". It is yes or no, and nothing else.

points.label: why it deserves a type
points.text: A yes/no fact is so common that Java gives it its own type, with exactly two possible values.

points.label: later
points.text: These are also what decisions are built from. Every "if the door is locked" starts as one of these.

steps.instruction: boolean holds one of exactly two values.

points.label: boolean
points.text: The type. Same four parts as always: type, name, =, value.

points.label: true
points.text: One of only two values it can ever hold. The other is false.

points.label: lowercase, no quotes
points.text: true, not True and not "true". Java is strict about this.

points.label: alive
points.text: Naming it like a yes/no question makes the code read like English.

steps.instruction: Run it.
steps.after: One fact, on the panel.

steps.instruction: The player just died. Make the panel say so.
steps.hint: There is only one other value it could be.
steps.after: Two values, and you have now used both.

Alive:      true
Has key:    false
Quest done: true

points.text: Each yes/no answer needs its own boolean. They do not share.

points.text: hasKey = false is not "empty" or "unset". It is a definite no.

points.label: reading the panel
points.text: Alive and quest done, but no key. That is a complete picture of the player in three words.

steps.instruction: Careful: true and "true" look identical on screen.

points.label: same output
points.text: Both print true. Quotes never appear, so you cannot tell them apart by looking.

points.label: true
points.text: A boolean. Java understands it as a yes and can reason with it.

points.label: "true"
points.text: A String. Four letters that happen to spell true. Java cannot make a decision from it.

points.label: the others
points.text: 'T' is a char. 10.1 is a double. Only bare true and false are booleans.

steps.instruction: Which type is each value?
steps.why: Bare true/false → boolean. Double quotes → String. Single quotes around one character → char. A decimal → double.

points.text: "true" with quotes is a String. 't' is a char. 10.1 is a double. Only the bare words count.

lessons.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation
objectives: explain why the right-hand side of && or || is sometimes skipped
put a guard on the left so the right side is safe
work out which side of an expression actually runs

points.text: n is 0. Dividing by zero crashes a Java program instantly.
points.label: 10 / n

points.text: (n != 0) is false, and false && anything is false — so Java never looks at the right side.
points.label: but it did not

points.text: That is the name: stopping early because the answer is already decided.
points.label: short-circuit

points.text: It is not an optimisation you can ignore. It is what keeps the division from ever happening.
points.label: you rely on this

steps.instruction: && stops the moment it finds a false.

steps.after: The guard on the left protected the division on the right.
steps.instruction: Run it. A divide by zero that never divides.

steps.why: || only needs one true and it found one immediately on the left, so the 5 / 0 is never evaluated. No crash.
steps.code: System.out.println(true || (5 / 0 == 0));
skills: explain why the right-hand side of && or || is sometimes skipped
steps.instruction: 5 / 0 would crash. Does this?

points.text: && gives up on the first false. || gives up on the first true.
points.label: mirror image

points.text: This is true, so || already knows the whole thing is true.
points.label: (n == 0)

points.text: The division on the right never runs, for the same reason as before.
points.label: skipped again

steps.instruction: || stops the moment it finds a true.

steps.after: Same protection, opposite operator.
steps.instruction: Run it.

points.text: Java always evaluates the left side first. Always.
points.label: left to right

points.text: The check that makes the other side safe has to come first.
points.label: guard on the left

points.text: (10 / n > 1) && (n != 0) crashes when n is 0 — the division runs before anything checks it.
points.label: swap them and it breaks

points.text: With short-circuiting, the ORDER of your conditions is part of whether the program works.
points.label: so

steps.instruction: Which side you put things on is now a real decision.

points.text: Two different-looking lines, one answer. That is the point of the law.

points.text: Capital S. It is the odd one out among the types — the rest are lowercase.

points.text: Always. Single quotes make a char, which holds exactly one character.

points.text: The user typed exactly "cat", and == still said false.
points.label: look at that

points.text: For Strings it asks "are these the same object in memory?", which is almost never what you mean.
Asks "are these the same characters?" — the actual question. It said true.
points.label: .equals()

points.text: Text is compared with .equals(). Numbers and booleans still use ==.
points.label: the rule

steps.instruction: To compare text, use .equals() — not ==.

steps.after: Same letters, different answer. That is why .equals() exists.
skills: explain why == is the wrong way to compare text
steps.instruction: Run it and watch == get it wrong.

steps.why: Java quietly reuses identical text written directly in the code, so both names point at the same one and == says true. It looks like == works — and that is exactly the trap. The moment the text comes from the user it says false. Use .equals() and you never have to think about this.
skills: explain why == is the wrong way to compare text
